loop.title: A control loop: drum level
caption: One loop, from the process and back to it. The transmitter measures the level and sends it as a current. caption: Output against input for three faulty transmitters. The grey line is the ideal one. A zero error shifts every point by the same amount. A span error is nothing at the bottom and largest at the top. With hysteresis the rising and falling readings are different.

In the second it starts at the right point and falls away towards the top (span error). In the third the rising and falling readings form a loop around the ideal line (hysteresis).

caption: Move the slider to change the input current. The flapper hangs from a hinge; the coil pulls it up towards the nozzle. vibwave.title: Peak, peak-to-peak and RMS
caption: One cycle of a pure sine-wave vibration. Peak is from the centre line to the top. Peak-to-peak is from bottom to top, twice the peak. RMS is 0.707 times the peak. These ratios hold for a sine wave only.

dva.title: The same velocity at different frequencies
caption: A vibration of 5 mm/s at every frequency. At low frequency this takes a large displacement and little acceleration. At high frequency the displacement shrinks to almost nothing and the acceleration becomes large. This is why slow machines are judged by displacement, fast effects by acceleration, and most machines in between by velocity.

title: Start here
goals: Know what this course covers, who it is for, and how to use it.

q: A guess before you start. A transmitter sends 12 mA on a 4–20 mA signal. Where is the measurement in its range?

why: 12 ÷ 20 = 60% would be right if the signal started at 0 mA. It starts at 4 mA. Module 4 covers this.
Right. The signal runs from 4 to 20 mA, 16 mA in all. 12 mA is 8 mA above the start: 8 ÷ 16 = 50%. Module 4 covers this.
Milliamps are not percent. The signal runs from 4 mA (0%) to 20 mA (100%).

p: This course is for the people who keep the plant's measurements and control loops working: instrument technicians and I&C engineers. It explains how a signal gets from the process to the DCS screen and back to a valve, and what you can measure with a multimeter at each point on the way.
The operators' view of instruments (what a transmitter is, how drum level is measured, alarms and trips) is in
(course 2), Module 7. Read that first if those words are new. This course goes one level deeper: inside the loop.
By the end you should be able to:

ul: Sketch a control loop and name every part between the process and the final element.
Convert between percent, engineering units, mA, volts across 250 Ω and psi, in both directions.
Use a multimeter on a live loop without disturbing it, and say what each reading tells you.
Explain how strain gauges, RTDs, capacitance cells, LVDTs, speed pickups and eddy-current probes turn a physical change into an electrical one.
Explain what amplifiers, filters, comparators and converters do to a signal.
Check a control valve with its I/P converter or positioner.
Read a vibration value, say which sensor made it, and check a proximity probe's gap voltage.
Find a fault in a 4–20 mA loop step by step.

cards: Each module opens with a question before any teaching. Answer it anyway.
Worked examples show one step at a time. Calculate each step before you reveal it.
Every wrong answer tells you why. Retry until each one is right.
A short daily drill on the terms. Five minutes a day.

p: Take the

text: Yes. A valve must not move by itself.

text: Probably not. The level is above the setpoint, so the controller is reducing the feed.
why: Right. That is a closed loop at work: PV above SP, so the output goes down. First compare PV and SP, then decide if something is wrong.

case: A steam pressure loop: PT → DCS controller → control valve. The operator says "the valve is hunting" (opening and closing all the time). Where in the loop do you look?
steps: Put the controller in manual with a fixed output. Now the loop is open: the valve gets a steady signal.
If the valve still moves with a steady signal, the fault is after the controller: positioner, I/P converter, air supply or the valve itself.
If the valve is still but the pressure reading still swings, look at the measurement: the process itself, the impulse line or the transmitter.

Then each half is healthy and the hunting comes from the loop as a whole: controller tuning, or a valve that sticks and then jumps. Opening the loop told you which half to work on before you touched a single wire.

p: To judge a point, turn its error into percent of span:
For a 4–20 mA output the span is 16 mA, so

case: A pressure transmitter is ranged 0–160 bar. The tolerance is ±0.25% of span. As found: 4.00, 8.03, 12.06, 16.09 and 20.12 mA. Does it pass, and what is wrong with it?
steps: 0.25% of 16 mA = 0.04 mA. Every point must be within ±0.04 mA of the ideal value.
Ideal values are 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20 mA. The errors are 0.00, +0.03, +0.06, +0.09 and +0.12 mA.
The 50%, 75% and 100% points are outside ±0.04 mA. It fails. The largest error is 0.12 ÷ 16 = 0.75% of span.
Zero is right and the error grows evenly with the input: a span error. Record the as-found values, adjust the span, and run all five points again up and down.

q: A transmitter is ranged −50 to +150 °C. What is its span?

why: That is the upper range value. Span = URV − LRV.
Subtracting a negative number adds: 150 + 50.

q: At 50% input a transmitter should give 12.00 mA. It gives 12.08 mA. What is the error in percent of span?

why: 0.08 is the error in mA. Divide by the 16 mA span.
That divides by 12 mA (the reading). The span is 16 mA.

q: Going up, a transmitter reads 12.00 mA at 50%. Coming down from 100%, it reads 12.07 mA at the same 50%. This is:

why: The same input gives a different output depending on the direction it was reached from.
A zero error would be the same in both directions.
Drift is a slow change over a long time.

q: Why do you write down the as-found readings before adjusting?

text: They show how far the instrument had drifted, and whether past readings can be trusted.
why: Right. Without as-found data nobody can tell if the plant ran on a wrong measurement, or how often the instrument needs checking.

text: They are needed to set the span.
why: The span is set from the reference, not from old readings.

text: There is no reason if the as-left readings are good.
why: The as-found record is the main result of a calibration.

q: Two transmitters measure the same steady pressure. A reads 80.4, 80.4, 80.4 bar. B reads 79.8, 80.3, 80.1 bar. The true value is 80.0 bar. Which statement is right?

text: A repeats better, but it has an offset of 0.4 bar.
why: A is repeatable and wrong by a steady amount, which calibration can correct. B scatters, which calibration cannot correct.

text: A is more accurate because it always shows the same value.
why: Showing the same value is repeatability. A is 0.4 bar off.

text: B is useless because its readings change.
why: B's average is close to the true value. Its weakness is repeatability.

q: Guess: you want to know the current in a running 4–20 mA loop, but you are not allowed to open it. The DCS input has a 250 Ω resistor. What can you do?

text: Nothing. Current can only be measured in series.
why: Directly, yes. But a known resistor in the loop turns the current into a voltage you can measure.

text: Measure the voltage across the 250 Ω resistor and divide by 250.
why: Right. Ohm's law: I = V ÷ R. 3.00 V across 250 Ω is 12.0 mA. The meter is across the resistor, so the loop stays closed.

text: Measure the resistance of the loop.
why: Never use the ohms range on a live circuit. The reading is meaningless and the meter injects its own current.

p: In a series circuit the current is the same at every point. So the DCS receives exactly the current that the transmitter sets, however long the cable is and whatever its resistance. A voltage signal would lose part of itself along the cable.

A current loop is also hard to disturb. Interference from nearby power cables induces small voltages in the signal cable. The transmitter controls the current and simply changes its own voltage a little to keep the current where it should be. Twisted pairs and a cable shield, earthed at one end only (normally in the cabinet), keep most of the interference out in the first place.

goals: Explain how a capacitance cell and a capacitance level probe work.
Explain how an LVDT measures position and what its output looks like.
Tell an inductive proximity switch from a capacitive one.

q: Guess: an LVDT on a valve stem gives zero output. What does that tell you?

why: Zero is the middle of the LVDT's stroke, not the end.

text: Either the core is exactly in the centre, or the LVDT has no excitation.
why: Right. Both give zero. Check the excitation voltage before you believe the position.
Zero is a normal output at the null position.

p: Two metal plates facing each other form a capacitor. Its capacitance depends on three things:

p: Change any one of the three and you have a sensor. The capacitances are small, picofarads, so the electronics sit close to the sensor and measure with an AC signal.

In a capacitance DP cell a thin metal diaphragm sits between two fixed plates. Pressure on one side moves the diaphragm a few hundredths of a millimetre towards one plate and away from the other. One capacitance rises and the other falls. The transmitter measures the difference, which makes the cell sensitive and cancels most temperature effects, in the same way a bridge does.

A rod in a tank and the tank wall (or a tube around the rod) form a long capacitor. As liquid replaces air between them, the capacitance rises in a straight line with the level. For a liquid that does not conduct, such as oil, a bare rod is used. For water the rod is insulated, and the insulation is the gap.
The reading depends on the liquid: a probe calibrated for one oil is wrong for another. Build-up on the rod also reads as level.
The

Core moved: the output amplitude is proportional to the distance from the centre, and its phase tells the side.
Nothing touches the core, so there is no wear, and the resolution is limited only by the electronics.
It needs AC excitation, typically a few volts at 1 to 10 kHz, and a demodulator that turns the AC output into a DC signal with a sign.

p: LVDTs report the position of turbine control and stop valves to the turbine controller, and measure casing and differential expansion. They are passive: with the excitation missing, the output is zero wherever the core is. On a simple position loop that can look like "valve at mid-stroke" instead of a fault, so check the excitation first.
A proximity switch detects that something is near, without touching it, and gives an on/off signal. It replaces a mechanical limit switch.

why: Correct. That gives zero at the centre and a signal that grows on either side.

case: A feed pump has a 30-tooth speed wheel with a magnetic pickup. The DCS shows 0 rpm although the pump is running. With a meter on the pickup wires in the cabinet you measure 1.8 V AC at 1490 Hz. What does that tell you?

rpm = 1490 × 60 ÷ 30 = 2980 rpm. A believable speed for the pump.

q: A wheel has 120 teeth and the shaft runs at 1500 rpm. What frequency does the pickup give?

why: That divides by the teeth. Multiply teeth by turns per second.
Divide by 60 to go from per minute to per second.

q: Which pickup can show that a shaft has really stopped?

why: Its voltage falls to nothing at low speed, long before standstill.
It gives full-size pulses at any speed, down to zero.
Hall-effect and eddy-current pickups work down to zero speed.

q: Why is a Schmitt trigger used on a pickup signal?

why: It does not make the signal larger.

text: To turn a noisy, rounded signal into clean pulses without extra false pulses.
why: Its two switching levels (hysteresis) ignore small ripples.
It only shapes pulses.

q: A single notch on a shaft at 600 rpm is measured by counting pulses for 1 second. How coarse is the result?

why: That would be true with 60 pulses per turn.
600 rpm is 10 pulses per second. One pulse more or less is one tenth: 60 rpm. Timing each turn is the better method here.
Counting few pulses gives a coarse result, not a fine one.

q: Why does overspeed protection use three pickups with two-out-of-three voting?

text: Three pickups are more accurate than one.
why: Accuracy is not the reason.

text: One failed pickup can neither cause a false trip nor stop a real one.
why: Right: the protection stays both safe and available with one channel failed.

text: Each pickup measures a different shaft.
why: They look at the same wheel.

Air opens this valve, so without air the spring closes it. That is its fail position.

The packing affects the valve travel, not the converter's output pressure.

why: Right. Only a probe that measures the shaft relative to the bearing sees that movement.
They are the more expensive system.

p: Every running machine shakes a little. A vibration reading does not name a fault. It tells you that something is making the machine move, and unbalance, misalignment, a loose foot, a worn bearing and a rub each do that in their own way. p: This course was written from general training material: slide decks and hand-outs on measurement, signal conditioning, converters and vibration. Nothing was copied from them. These are the places where that material is wrong or unclear, and what the course teaches instead, for readers who have the same documents.

issues: One deck files a silicon pressure sensor of the piezoresistive kind (a strain-gauge bridge on a diaphragm) under the self-generating sensors. It is passive: without excitation it gives nothing. The piezoelectric accelerometer in the same list is rightly active. (Module 1)

A hand-out on eddy-current testing gives the formula for the standard depth of penetration without the factor π. The full formula is δ = 1 ÷ √(π f µ σ). Its unit for conductivity is also not a conductivity unit, and it treats the permeability of non-magnetic metals as 1 where it means their relative permeability. (Module 11)

A deck on signal conditioning, where it lists the properties of the ideal amplifier, names the wrong pair of voltages as equal. It is the two inputs that sit at the same voltage, and only when feedback is connected. (Module 8)

A note on 4–20 mA reasons that the low power of the signal makes it safe in hazardous areas. A loop is only safe there when it is designed and certified for it (for example intrinsically safe, with a barrier). (Module 4)
How far a current signal reaches
The same note gives a fixed distance for error-free transmission. There is no such distance. What counts is the loop resistance against the supply voltage. (Module 4)

A summary of meter use describes the resistance between the leads as very low in general. That holds only on the current ranges. On the voltage ranges it is very high, as the same deck explains elsewhere. (Module 3)
Two slides of one deck give different ranges for the gauge factor of metal gauges. For the usual foil gauges it is close to 2. (Module 5)

One deck counts high sensitivity among the strengths of the LVDT and low sensitivity among its limits. An LVDT is sensitive; its real limits are that it needs AC excitation and a demodulator. (Module 6)
I/P converter on loss of signal
A hand-out uses an unusual term for what the output does when the signal fails. Said plainly: with no current the output falls to its minimum and the valve goes to its fail position. (Module 10)
The fixed ratios between peak, RMS and average are given without the condition that they hold for a sine wave only. (Module 11)
